results.location: 3.2 Spacetime Pyramid Modeling for Unified Generation
results.content:
Each video is decomposed into sequential clips $\{c_1, c_2, \cdots, c_N\}$. We regard the first frame as $c_1$ (i.e., $T = 1$) to encode video main static appearance cues specifically and other clips share an equal duration $T > 1$. Each clip is represented as a 3D volume pyramid with $K$ scales, each denoted by residual token blocks $r_k$ of dimensions $(T, h_k, w_k)$. [...] Mathematically, the clip tokens are generated auto-regressively across scales as:

$$
p(r_1^1, \ldots, r_K^1) = \prod_{k=1}^{K} p(r_k^1 \mid r_1^1, \ldots, r_{k-1}^1, \psi(t)),
\tag{1}
$$
results.route_rationale: A factorisation identity for a joint probability over the $K$ pyramid scales of one clip. Formalisable as the discrete chain rule, i.e. a telescoping product of prefix marginals.

lean_result.reasoning: Formalised the mathematical content of Eq. (1): the chain-rule factorisation of the intra-clip joint over scales. Writing $m(k)$ for the probability of the length-$k$ prefix $r_1^1,\ldots,r_k^1$ given $\psi(t)$ (so $m(0)=1$ and $m(K)$ is the left-hand side), the $k$-th factor of the right-hand side is by definition of conditional probability $p(r_k^1 \mid r_{<k}^1, \psi(t)) = m(k)/m(k-1)$. The claim is then the telescoping identity $\prod_{k \in [0,K)} m(k+1)/m(k) = m(K)$, assumed under the genuine standing hypothesis that prefix probabilities are nonzero (without it the conditionals the paper writes are not defined at all, so this is not a strengthening of the claim). Lean proved it by induction on $K$; clean compile, no `sorry`, standard Mathlib axioms only. One notational slip worth recording but not flaggable: the left-hand side is written $p(r_1^1,\ldots,r_K^1)$ without conditioning on $\psi(t)$ while every right-hand factor conditions on it, so read literally the two sides differ unless the tokens are independent of the text. Eq. (1) is plainly intended as $p(r_1^1,\ldots,r_K^1 \mid \psi(t))$, and under that reading the identity is exactly what Lean verified. Dropped-conditioning notation of this kind is standard-practice sloppiness, not a derivation-invalidating error.

lean.formal_statement:
theorem infinityStar_eq1_chain_rule
    (K : ℕ) (m : ℕ → ℝ) (h0 : m 0 = 1) (hne : ∀ k, m k ≠ 0) :
    ∏ k ∈ Finset.range K, (m (k + 1) / m k) = m K := by
  induction K with
  | zero => simp [h0]
  | succ n ih =>
    rw [Finset.prod_range_succ, ih]
    have h := hne n
    field_simp

results.location: 3.2 Spacetime Pyramid Modeling for Unified Generation
results.content:
For inter-clip predictions, clips are generated sequentially conditioned on prior clip predictions and the text input in an autoregressive manner. In this way, we could generate infinitely long videos theoretically. Formally, the autoregressive likelihood of the whole video can be expressed as:

$$
p(r_1^1, \ldots, r_K^N) = \prod_{c=1}^{N} \prod_{k=1}^{K} p(r_k^c \mid r_1^c, \ldots, r_{k-1}^c, \psi(t)),
\tag{2}
$$
results.route_rationale: The paper's formal statement of its whole-video likelihood. The conditioning sets on the right-hand side contain no block from any preceding clip, so the identity is a crisp, formally testable claim about factorisation — and a candidate for refutation rather than proof.

lean_result.reasoning:
Every factor on the right-hand side of Eq. (2) conditions only on $r_1^c, \ldots, r_{k-1}^c$ — blocks of the *same* clip $c$ — together with $\psi(t)$. No superscript ranges over earlier clips. Applying Eq. (1) to the inner product therefore collapses the right-hand side exactly:

$$\prod_{k=1}^{K} p(r_k^c \mid r_1^c, \ldots, r_{k-1}^c, \psi(t)) = p(r_1^c, \ldots, r_K^c \mid \psi(t)),$$

so Eq. (2) asserts $p(r^1, \ldots, r^N \mid \psi(t)) = \prod_{c=1}^{N} p(r^c \mid \psi(t))$ — that the clips are mutually independent given the text. That is false for a general joint law, and false precisely in the regime the paper models: the sentence immediately above Eq. (2) says clips are "generated sequentially conditioned on prior clip predictions", and §3.4's spacetime sparse attention explicitly attends to the last scale of the preceding clip, both of which require inter-clip dependence.

Lean refuted the identity by exhibiting a witness: with $N = 2$, $K = 1$ and blocks valued in $\{\text{true}, \text{false}\}$, take the perfectly correlated law $q(b_1, b_2) = \tfrac{1}{2}$ if $b_1 = b_2$ and $0$ otherwise. It is nonnegative with total mass $1$, yet $q(\text{true}, \text{true}) = \tfrac{1}{2}$ while the product of its marginals is $\tfrac{1}{2} \cdot \tfrac{1}{2} = \tfrac{1}{4}$. Clean compile, no `sorry`, standard axioms only; the witness was independently re-checked numerically ($\sum q = 1$, joint $= 1/2$, product of marginals $= 1/4$). The intended equation is evidently $p(r_1^1, \ldots, r_K^N) = \prod_{c}\prod_{k} p(r_k^c \mid r^{<c}, r_1^c, \ldots, r_{k-1}^c, \psi(t))$; the conditioning on $r^{<c}$ has been dropped from the displayed formula.
contradiction_locations: Eq. (2), conditioning set of each factor
preceding sentence: "clips are generated sequentially conditioned on prior clip predictions"
§3.4 Spacetime Sparse Attention: "we only attend to the last scale of the preceding clip"

lean.formal_statement:
theorem infinityStar_eq2_refuted :
    ∃ q : Bool → Bool → ℝ,
      (∀ b₁ b₂, 0 ≤ q b₁ b₂) ∧
      (∑ b₁ : Bool, ∑ b₂ : Bool, q b₁ b₂) = 1 ∧
      q true true ≠ (∑ b₂ : Bool, q true b₂) * (∑ b₁ : Bool, q b₁ true) := by
  refine ⟨fun b₁ b₂ => if b₁ = b₂ then (1 : ℝ) / 2 else 0, ?_, ?_, ?_⟩
  · intro b₁ b₂; by_cases h : b₁ = b₂ <;> simp [h]
  · simp
  · simp

results.content:
Stochastic Quantizer Depth. [...] To alleviate this problem, we propose a regularization called stochastic quantizer depth. During training, each one of the last $N$ scales has a probability $p$ of being discarded.

In this way, there are $2^N$ possible scale schedules during training. This requires the tokenizer to reduce the reliance on last scales and store more information in tokens of early scales.
results.route_rationale: A closed-form combinatorial count. Formalisable as the cardinality of the keep/discard decision space over the $N$ droppable scales.

lean_result.reasoning: A realised schedule is determined by the independent keep/discard decision on each of the $N$ droppable scales, i.e. by an element of $\{\text{keep}, \text{discard}\}^N$, equivalently by the subset of discarded scales. Lean verified both counts equal $2^N$ for every $N$ (`Fintype.card (Fin N → Bool) = 2 ^ N` and the power-set cardinality). Clean compile, no `sorry`, standard axioms only. The count is correct as stated; note it is the number of *reachable* schedules, not the number of equiprobable ones — a schedule discarding $j$ of the $N$ scales has probability $p^j(1-p)^{N-j}$, so for $p \notin \{0, 1\}$ all $2^N$ are reachable with positive probability, which is what the paper's argument needs. The paper does not claim uniformity, so there is nothing to flag.

lean.formal_statement:
theorem infinityStar_sqd_schedule_count (N : ℕ) :
    Fintype.card (Fin N → Bool) = 2 ^ N ∧
    (Finset.univ : Finset (Finset (Fin N))).card = 2 ^ N := by
  constructor
  · simp
  · simp

results.location: 2.3 Discrete Video Tokenizers — Infinity for Image Generation
results.content: To cover images of various sizes, Infinity pre-defines a list of token block sizes {(h1, w1), ...(hK, wK)}, called scale schedule. The size (hi, wi) in scale schedule grows as i increases, forming a pyramid-like structure [...] the tokenizer first encodes the raw images into compact latents, then transforms latents into K discrete residual token blocks (r1, r2, ..., rK) using a bitwise multi-scale residual quantizer [13]. Each token block ri consists of hi × wi discrete tokens of d-dim with vocabulary size of 2^d. Then in the second stage, a VAR Transformer is trained to predict next residual token block rk conditioned on text embedding ψ(t) and former token blocks r<k. Formally, in each step, VAR Transformer predicts a conditional probability p(rk|r<k, ψ(t)). During the inference, Infinity generates an image by running the VAR Transformer K times autoregressively, merging the predicted tokens and running the tokenizer decoder once.
results.route_rationale: Definitional recap of prior work: block counts, the $2^d$ vocabulary induced by $d$-dimensional bitwise tokens, and the per-step conditional. Checkable by inspection; asserts no non-trivial theorem.

verify_math_result.reasoning: Every quantity is internally consistent. A $d$-dimensional bitwise token ranges over $\{0,1\}^d$, giving exactly $2^d$ codewords, so "$d$-dim with vocabulary size of $2^d$" is correct. A block of $h_i \times w_i$ such tokens, $K$ blocks, and $K$ autoregressive steps match: one Transformer call per block. The per-step conditional $p(r_k \mid r_{<k}, \psi(t))$ is consistent with the chain-rule factorisation of Eq. (1), and a single decoder call after merging is consistent with residual quantisation (the merged latent is the sum of the residuals). No algebraic, sign, or domain issue.

results.content: After inserting the patchify and unpatchify layers between Wan 2.1 VAE’s encoder and decoder, we obtain a video tokenizer with a compression rate of 4 × 16 × 16 and a latent dimension of 64. BSQ quantization is adopted with a vocabulary of size 2^64. In contrast to using a vocabulary of size 2^64 for all scales, we use a vocabulary of size 2^16 for the former small scales and 2^64 for the latter large scales. We empirically find that it boosts convergence and has a negligible impact on reconstruction quality.
results.route_rationale: Dimension/vocabulary arithmetic over the tokenizer configuration; inspection-level consistency check against the $2^d$ rule stated in §2.3.

verify_math_result.reasoning: Consistent with the paper's own $2^d$ rule: a latent dimension of $64$ under binary spherical quantisation gives $d = 64$ bits per token and hence a vocabulary of $2^{64} \approx 1.84 \times 10^{19}$, exactly as stated. The mixed scheme — $2^{16}$ on early scales, $2^{64}$ on late ones — is coherent for BSQ, where a smaller vocabulary corresponds to quantising only a $16$-dimensional sub-block of the $64$-dimensional latent, and $2^{16} = 65536$ divides the full code space. The $4 \times 16 \times 16$ compression rate is a configuration statement, independent of the vocabulary arithmetic, and does not conflict with it. No algebraic or domain error.

results.content:
[Abstract] Without extra optimizations, our model generates a 5s, 720p video approximately 10× faster than leading diffusion-based methods.

[§1] Besides, InfinityStar shows a great advantage in terms of speed. Using visual tokenizers of the same compression rate, InfinityStar achieves a 10× reduction in inference latency relative to leading diffusion models.

[§4.5] Even without employing stronger compression, InfinityStar achieves a 32× speedup over Wan-2.1.

[Tab. 6] | Diffusion | Wan 2.1 [28] | 14B | 5 | 81 | 720p | 1864 | 1 |  …  | AR | InfinityStar | 8B | 5 | 81 | 720p | 58 | 32 |
results.route_rationale: Cross-section consistency of the paper's headline speedup multiplier. The underlying measurements are experimental, so this is not formalisable — but the two reported multipliers for the same configuration are directly comparable by arithmetic.

verify_math_result.reasoning:
The paper reports two mutually inconsistent values for the same quantity — the inference-latency speedup over leading diffusion models at 5 s, 720p — and each is presented under the same qualification, so they cannot both be right.

Table 6 and §4.5 give $1864/58 = 32.1$, stated as "$32\times$ speedup over Wan-2.1" and explicitly qualified "Even without employing stronger compression". The Abstract gives "approximately $10\times$ faster than leading diffusion-based methods" for exactly the same 5 s, 720p configuration, qualified "Without extra optimizations"; §1 repeats $10\times$ under the qualification "Using visual tokenizers of the same compression rate". The two qualifications coincide: §4.5 asserts its $32\times$ is *not* attributable to stronger compression, which is precisely the condition under which §1 reports $10\times$. The figures differ by a factor of $3.2$, and no third measurement in the paper supports $10\times$ — Table 6 is the only latency table and contains no diffusion baseline whose ratio to $58$ s is near $10$ (that would require a baseline latency of roughly $580$ s; the only diffusion entry is $1864$ s).

Supporting detail, not the basis of the finding: the paper's tokenizer is specified in §4.1 as $4 \times 16 \times 16$, a *higher* spatial compression than the Wan 2.1 VAE it is built from, which makes §4.5's "even without employing stronger compression" additionally hard to sustain and suggests $10\times$ was the compression-normalised figure that §4.5 then overstated.

Severity is minor: the efficiency advantage is real and substantial under either number, and the Abstract understates rather than inflates it, so no conclusion of the paper is overturned. But one of the two headline multipliers is wrong as printed and warrants correction.
contradiction_locations: Abstract: "approximately 10× faster than leading diffusion-based methods"
§1: "a 10× reduction in inference latency relative to leading diffusion models"
§4.5: "Even without employing stronger compression, InfinityStar achieves a 32× speedup over Wan-2.1"

results.location: 3.4 Spacetime Autoregressive Transformer — Semantic Scale Repetition
results.content:
Concretely, if a clip pyramid comprises $K$ scale tuples, we repeat the first $K_s$ tuples $N$ times, thereby reinforcing the semantic-level representations. In this way, every earlier residual $r_k$ undergoes multiple rounds of refinement, improving the generation quality of semantics and the performance in complex scenarios with large motion. Given that the tokens at these early scales account for only a small fraction of the total token count, the additional computational overhead incurred by repeating them is negligible.

[§4.1] semantic scale repetition repeats the first 7 scales 6 times.
results.route_rationale: The negligible-overhead claim is a quantitative statement about token counts, but it depends on a scale schedule the paper never specifies, so there is nothing self-contained to formalise.

verify_math_result.reasoning: The construction is well specified ($K$ scale tuples, the first $K_s$ repeated $N$ times; §4.1 instantiates $K_s = 7$, $N = 6$) and the overhead claim is qualitatively sound: repetition adds $(N-1)\sum_{k \le K_s} h_k w_k T$ tokens against a total $\sum_{k \le K} h_k w_k T$, and in a geometric-style pyramid the early-scale terms are a small fraction, consistent with §3.3's observation that "there are only a few tokens in the early scales, while there are tens of thousands of tokens in the last scales". But the paper never publishes the spacetime scale schedule $\{(T, h_k, w_k)\}_{k=1}^{K}$ or even $K$, so the overhead fraction cannot be evaluated and "negligible" cannot be confirmed or contradicted from the snippet. Nothing here is provably invalid; it is simply not checkable. Recorded separately, and not a mathematical error: the symbol $N$ is overloaded across the method section — the number of clips in §3.2, the number of droppable trailing scales in §3.3, and the repetition count here. That is a notation collision, which this verifier does not flag.

results.location: 3.4 Spacetime Autoregressive Transformer — Spacetime Sparse Attention
results.content: Spacetime Sparse Attention. […] As shown on the left of Fig. 2, Infinity [13] employs a block-wise causal mask for single-pyramid modeling. Switti [27] verifies that conditioning next-scale predictions solely on inputs from preceding scales is sufficient, resulting in a sparser attention mask as in the middle of Fig. 2. For long video generation, it’s necessary to attend to history tokens to achieve temporal consistency. However, attending full history leads to an explosively long sequence. Considering each clip corresponds to 5s, which is sufficient to maintain temporal consistency, here we only attend to the last scale of the preceding clip. Finally, we obtain a highly sparse attention as shown in Fig. 2 (right). Our spacetime sparse attention reduces attention computational overhead during training and inference, maintaining comparable or improved performance relative to full attention.
results.route_rationale: An architectural/modelling description whose claims are about empirical cost and quality rather than a theorem; no crisp formal content and the attention mask is defined only by reference to a figure.

verify_math_result.reasoning: The cost claim is directionally coherent — restricting each clip's cross-clip context to the single last scale of its predecessor bounds the attended history by a constant per clip instead of letting it grow linearly in clip index, which does reduce attention cost from quadratic in total sequence length toward linear in the number of clips — and Table 5 is consistent with it. But the mask is specified only by reference to Fig. 2 (right), an image not available as text, and the quality claim ("comparable or improved performance relative to full attention", attributed in §4.4 to reduced exposure bias) is an empirical hypothesis about trained models, not a mathematical assertion. There is no self-contained statement here that could be proved or refuted. One observation recorded without flagging: this design is exactly the inter-clip dependence that Eq. (2) fails to express, which corroborates the paper::EQUATION::1 finding that the omission of $r^{<c}$ from Eq. (2) is a transcription error rather than the intended model.

findings.evidence:
Eq. (2), the paper's formal statement of its whole-video autoregressive likelihood, conditions every factor only on blocks of the **same** clip $c$ plus the text embedding. No index ranges over preceding clips. Collapsing the inner product with the paper's own Eq. (1) gives

$$\prod_{k=1}^{K} p(r_k^c \mid r_1^c, \ldots, r_{k-1}^c, \psi(t)) = p(r_1^c, \ldots, r_K^c \mid \psi(t)),$$

so Eq. (2) asserts $p(r^1, \ldots, r^N \mid \psi(t)) = \prod_{c=1}^{N} p(r^c \mid \psi(t))$ — mutual independence of the clips given the text. Lean refuted this: with $N = 2$, $K = 1$ and binary blocks, the perfectly correlated law $q(b_1,b_2) = \tfrac12$ if $b_1 = b_2$ and $0$ otherwise is a valid distribution ($\sum q = 1$, $q \ge 0$) with $q(\text{true},\text{true}) = \tfrac12$ but product of marginals $\tfrac12 \cdot \tfrac12 = \tfrac14$. The refutation compiles clean with no `sorry` and only the standard Mathlib axioms.

The equation also contradicts its own surrounding text: the sentence immediately preceding it says clips are "generated sequentially conditioned on prior clip predictions", and §3.4's spacetime sparse attention attends to the last scale of the preceding clip. The intended formula is evidently $p(r_1^1,\ldots,r_K^N) = \prod_c \prod_k p(r_k^c \mid r^{<c}, r_1^c, \ldots, r_{k-1}^c, \psi(t))$; the conditioning on $r^{<c}$ has been dropped. As printed, the headline equation defining the model's likelihood is false, and under it the paper's central claim of temporal autoregression across clips would be vacuous.

The paper gives two irreconcilable values for its headline inference-latency speedup over leading diffusion models at the same 5 s, 720p setting. Table 6 reports $1864$ s for Wan 2.1 against $58$ s for InfinityStar, i.e. $1864/58 = 32.1$, and §4.5 states a "$32\times$ speedup". The Abstract states "approximately $10\times$ faster" for that same configuration, and §1 repeats $10\times$. The qualifications do not separate the two claims — §1's $10\times$ holds "[u]sing visual tokenizers of the same compression rate" while §4.5 asserts its $32\times$ is obtained "[e]ven without employing stronger compression", which is the same condition. The figures differ by a factor of $3.2$, and no measurement in the paper supports $10\times$: Table 6 is the only latency table, and a $10\times$ ratio against $58$ s would require a diffusion baseline near $580$ s, whereas the sole diffusion entry is $1864$ s. Supporting context: §4.1 specifies a $4 \times 16 \times 16$ tokenizer, a higher spatial compression than the Wan 2.1 VAE it inherits from, which makes "even without employing stronger compression" additionally difficult to sustain. Severity is minor — the efficiency advantage is substantial under either figure and the Abstract understates rather than inflates it — but one of the two printed multipliers is wrong.
findings.exact_quote: Without extra optimizations, our model generates a 5s, 720p video approximately 10× faster than leading diffusion-based methods.

summary:
Thirteen mathematical objects were extracted from InfinityStar and all thirteen were checked: three were routed to Lean 4 (sharing the pre-existing, multi-paper `MATH_VERIFICATION/Paper` project) and ten to informal review. The paper carries very little formal mathematics — two displayed equations and a handful of quantitative claims — so the Lean queue was short but landed on the paper's central formulae.

**What Lean settled.** Two `PASSED`, one `REFUTED`, zero `FAILED`, so no informal fallbacks were required.

- Eq. (1), the intra-clip factorisation across pyramid scales, is correct: formalised as the telescoping product $\prod_{k} m(k)/m(k-1) = m(K)$ over prefix marginals and proved by induction. (A notational slip was recorded but not flagged: the left-hand side omits the conditioning on $\psi(t)$ that every right-hand factor carries.)
- §3.3's combinatorial claim that stochastic quantizer depth admits $2^N$ scale schedules is correct — Lean confirmed $|\{\text{keep},\text{discard}\}^N| = 2^N$.
- **Eq. (2) was formally refuted.** Every factor conditions only on blocks of the same clip, so by Eq. (1) the right-hand side collapses to $\prod_c p(r^c \mid \psi(t))$ — clip independence given the text. Lean exhibited a compiling counterexample (two perfectly correlated binary clips: joint $1/2$, product of marginals $1/4$). This contradicts the sentence directly above Eq. (2) and the whole spacetime-sparse-attention design, so it is a transcription error — the conditioning on $r^{<c}$ was dropped — rather than a flaw in the method. It is nonetheless the paper's headline likelihood, printed wrong, which drives the `CRITICAL_ERRORS` verdict.

**What informal review settled.** The reported statistics are unusually clean. The VBench aggregation $\text{Overall} = 0.8 \cdot \text{Quality} + 0.2 \cdot \text{Semantic}$ reproduces all eleven rows of Table 2 and all seven of Table 4 to within $\pm 0.006$, i.e. display rounding; every total-score pair quoted in §4.4's prose matches Table 4; Table 6's speedups follow from its latencies ($1864/58 = 32.1$, $354/58 = 6.1$); Table 5's $1.5\times$, $1.1\times$ and $1.5\times$ multipliers all follow from its timings; and the clip arithmetic reconciles exactly ($80$ frames at $16$ fps $= 5$ s, plus the static first frame $= 81$ frames, as in Table 6). The tokenizer configuration ($d = 64 \Rightarrow 2^{64}$ vocabulary) is self-consistent.

One numeric inconsistency was flagged at confidence $0.72$: the Abstract and §1 claim a $10\times$ latency advantage over leading diffusion models while §4.5 and Table 6 claim $32\times$ for the same 5 s/720p configuration under the same "no stronger compression / no extra optimizations" qualification. Nothing in the paper supports $10\times$. Severity is minor — the Abstract understates the measured advantage, so no conclusion is overturned.

**Not settled.** Two modelling snippets came back `UNVERIFIABLE`: the "negligible overhead" claim for semantic scale repetition (the spacetime scale schedule and $K$ are never published, so the overhead fraction cannot be evaluated) and the spacetime sparse attention description (the mask is defined only by reference to Fig. 2, and its quality claim is empirical). Neither contains anything provably invalid. Two non-flaggable issues are on record in the per-snippet reasoning: the symbol $N$ is overloaded across §3.2 (clip count), §3.3 (droppable trailing scales) and §3.4 (repetition count), and §4.4's running text writes "16f" where Table 5 says "161 frames".

**Verifier agreement.** The two verifiers did not disagree anywhere — no Lean result needed an informal second opinion, and the informal pass independently corroborated the Eq. (2) refutation by noting that §3.4's cross-clip attention is precisely the dependence Eq. (2) fails to express.

**Lean project.** `MATH_VERIFICATION/Paper` was reused, not created by this run (it is shared by every `paper.md` in the workspace and holds a built Mathlib plus other papers' proofs), so per `verify-math-lean`'s reuse rule it was kept rather than deleted. Only per-snippet scratch (`TMP.lean`, `claim.md`) was removed; the three proofs are saved as `Paper/Verified/paper__{EQUATION__0,EQUATION__1,MATHEMATICAL_MODEL__0}_2539opus5.lean`.
